PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php
# Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40, the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires.
But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40.
(Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)
...
Under the California Constitution, if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.

Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement.

S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election
The San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board’s endorsements for the California and S.F. Bay Area election on Nov. 3.
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) | Updated Nov. 2, 2026 4:37 p.m.
California’s November election is shaping up to be one of the most confusing in years for voters to navigate. There are 14 measures on the state ballot, many of them dense and extremely complicated tax policies. Unsurprisingly, polls show 80% of voters are frustrated and pessimistic about how this election will impact them. Voters in San Francisco and Oakland will also have to weigh in on hugely impactful charter reform ballot measures that could change the future of their cities.
In this kind of environment, details matter. And, yes, your vote matters.
The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board has spent months interviewing candidates, talking to experts, fact checking campaign promises and scrutinizing the issues in every statewide contest on the ballot, along with a group of consequential races in the Bay Area. These recommendations are made by Opinion writers and editors; newsroom reporters who cover the campaigns do not participate in endorsement decisions.
Below are the editorial board’s recommendations for the November 2026 election . We encourage readers to click through to the full endorsements to see the board’s reasoning and understand its decisions — so that you can be fully armed to make your own informed decisions.

California races
The editorial board recommends
Governor: Xavier Becerra Democrat Voting rights attorney
Why we're endorsing
The entire purpose of electing an experienced politician like Becerra is to feel confident that he will have the discernment to know which big ideas to go after and which to pass on, that he will arrive on the job with a meaningful, achievable agenda and actionable plans, and that he can communicate that agenda transparently and effectively to the public. We do not feel confident. All that said, Becerra’s Republican opponent, Steve Hilton — an ally of President Donald Trump — is no viable option.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-governor-race-22494871.php)
Lieutenant Governor: Fiona Ma Democrat State treasurer/CPA
Why we're endorsing
Fiona Ma comes with significant baggage — which is why she wasn’t our first choice for the role in the June primary. But she has the competence and experience to smoothly assume the duties of the state’s No. 2 office. Given the ramblings of her opponent, we cautiously recommend Ma for lieutenant governor.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/lieutenant-governor-california-state-election-22404751.php)
Secretary of State: Shirley Weber Democrat California secretary of state ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
California is no ocean of calm when it comes to elections. The need for steady and trustworthy leadership from our secretary of state cannot be understated. Shirley Weber’s breadth of experience, willingness to do the right thing and fierce advocacy for voting rights make her the strongest candidate.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/shirley-weber-secretary-state-california-22228493.php)
Controller: Malia Cohen Democrat State controller ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing

S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election
The San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board’s endorsements for the California and S.F. Bay Area election on Nov. 3.
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) | Updated Nov. 2, 2026 4:37 p.m.
California’s November election is shaping up to be one of the most confusing in years for voters to navigate. There are 14 measures on the state ballot, many of them dense and extremely complicated tax policies. Unsurprisingly, polls show 80% of voters are frustrated and pessimistic about how this election will impact them. Voters in San Francisco and Oakland will also have to weigh in on hugely impactful charter reform ballot measures that could change the future of their cities.
In this kind of environment, details matter. And, yes, your vote matters.
The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board has spent months interviewing candidates, talking to experts, fact checking campaign promises and scrutinizing the issues in every statewide contest on the ballot, along with a group of consequential races in the Bay Area. These recommendations are made by Opinion writers and editors; newsroom reporters who cover the campaigns do not participate in endorsement decisions.
Below are the editorial board’s recommendations for the November 2026 election . We encourage readers to click through to the full endorsements to see the board’s reasoning and understand its decisions — so that you can be fully armed to make your own informed decisions.

By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) | Updated Nov. 2, 2026 4:37 p.m.
California’s November election is shaping up to be one of the most confusing in years for voters to navigate. There are 14 measures on the state ballot, many of them dense and extremely complicated tax policies. Unsurprisingly, polls show 80% of voters are frustrated and pessimistic about how this election will impact them. Voters in San Francisco and Oakland will also have to weigh in on hugely impactful charter reform ballot measures that could change the future of their cities.
In this kind of environment, details matter. And, yes, your vote matters.
The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board has spent months interviewing candidates, talking to experts, fact checking campaign promises and scrutinizing the issues in every statewide contest on the ballot, along with a group of consequential races in the Bay Area. These recommendations are made by Opinion writers and editors; newsroom reporters who cover the campaigns do not participate in endorsement decisions.
Below are the editorial board’s recommendations for the November 2026 election . We encourage readers to click through to the full endorsements to see the board’s reasoning and understand its decisions — so that you can be fully armed to make your own informed decisions.

California races
The editorial board recommends
Governor: Xavier Becerra Democrat Voting rights attorney
Why we're endorsing
The entire purpose of electing an experienced politician like Becerra is to feel confident that he will have the discernment to know which big ideas to go after and which to pass on, that he will arrive on the job with a meaningful, achievable agenda and actionable plans, and that he can communicate that agenda transparently and effectively to the public. We do not feel confident. All that said, Becerra’s Republican opponent, Steve Hilton — an ally of President Donald Trump — is no viable option.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-governor-race-22494871.php)
Lieutenant Governor: Fiona Ma Democrat State treasurer/CPA
Why we're endorsing
Fiona Ma comes with significant baggage — which is why she wasn’t our first choice for the role in the June primary. But she has the competence and experience to smoothly assume the duties of the state’s No. 2 office. Given the ramblings of her opponent, we cautiously recommend Ma for lieutenant governor.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/lieutenant-governor-california-state-election-22404751.php)
Secretary of State: Shirley Weber Democrat California secretary of state ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
California is no ocean of calm when it comes to elections. The need for steady and trustworthy leadership from our secretary of state cannot be understated. Shirley Weber’s breadth of experience, willingness to do the right thing and fierce advocacy for voting rights make her the strongest candidate.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/shirley-weber-secretary-state-california-22228493.php)
Controller: Malia Cohen Democrat State controller ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
The State Controller’s Office is California’s internal auditor — empowered to investigate how state agencies and local governments are spending state funds. Overall, we think Cohen has made enough progress to merit another term. But Californians should stay watchful to ensure she keeps the positive momentum going.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/malia-cohen-state-controller-california-22242981.php)
Treasurer: Eleni Kounalakis Democrat Lieutenant governor
Why we're endorsing
The California state treasurer is the main banker, financier and asset manager for the world’s fourth-largest economy. With her thorough grasp of the treasurer’s complex duties and the political gravitas to get things done, Eleni Kounalakis deserves your vote.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-eleni-kounalakis-california-treasurer-22154455.php)
Attorney General: Rob Bonta Democrat Attorney general ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
In our endorsement interview, incumbent Rob Bonta’s calm, clear and concise grasp of the complexities and nuances of California law — honed through more than eight years in the state Assembly — surpassed that of most of the current gubernatorial candidates.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/rob-bonta-attorney-general-california-22194540.php)

Why we're endorsing
The insurance market has began to show signs of recovery. Insurers are finally starting to write new policies in the state. Electing a rash insurance commissioner could reverse that progress and cause the market to implode. Ben Allen has what it takes to hold insurers accountable and regulate their market conduct while also fostering the conditions necessary to keep the market stable.

The editorial board recommends
Proposition 1: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Befitting the broad consensus on California’s affordability crisis, Prop 1 has no formal opposition. The measure is the product of years of legislative sausage-making and is unwieldy. But the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait — and Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop1-california-housing-vote-22442444.php)
Proposition 2: Yes
Why we're endorsing
If used to the fullest extent, Prop 2 could improve California’s budget stability, permitting the state to cover about 50% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years. Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-2-money-california-22468892.php)
Proposition 3: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but also keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php)
Proposition 4: No
Why we're endorsing
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends on how it’s designed. Prop 4 has a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)
Proposition 5: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials. The process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)
Proposition 37: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Prop 37 promises to make it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership. Its scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change the state’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php)
Proposition 38: No
Why we're endorsing
Wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world? Prop 38 positions itself as such a balm. In fact, it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years. It would give billions to an institute co-founded by billionaire Michael Milken, also known as the “junk bond king,” who was pardoned by Trump in 2020.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Proposition 39: No
Why we're endorsing
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. But even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California, Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-proposition-39-voter-fraud-california-22463918.php)
Proposition 40: No
Why we're endorsing
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be. Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” If it backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. No one is coming to save us, and it won’t be the wealthy who suffer. California isn’t a lab rat. Voters shouldn’t allow our state to be treated like one.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Proposition 41: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund. But really it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)
Proposition 42: No
Why we're endorsing
Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what the backers of this measure would have you believe. In reality, it’s just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax. You don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php)
Proposition 43: No endorsement
Why we're endorsing
Despite commanding far less attention than the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a question reverberating throughout the nation: Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work? We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements California’s broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)
Proposition 44: No
Why we're endorsing
On its surface, everything about Prop 44 on California’s November ballot looks appealing. But it creates a complex administrative and legal regime that will drain limited staff time and resources from nonprofit clinics while distracting from patient care.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php)
Proposition 45: No
Why we're endorsing
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, and some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45. But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22468905.php)

Congress in the age of Trump is no place to learn on the job. Wahab is the only candidate prepared for the gravity of the moment.

Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials. The process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)
Proposition 37: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Prop 37 promises to make it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership. Its scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change the state’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php)
Proposition 38: No
Why we're endorsing
Wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world? Prop 38 positions itself as such a balm. In fact, it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years. It would give billions to an institute co-founded by billionaire Michael Milken, also known as the “junk bond king,” who was pardoned by Trump in 2020.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Proposition 39: No
Why we're endorsing
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. But even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California, Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-proposition-39-voter-fraud-california-22463918.php)
Proposition 40: No
Why we're endorsing
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be. Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” If it backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. No one is coming to save us, and it won’t be the wealthy who suffer. California isn’t a lab rat. Voters shouldn’t allow our state to be treated like one.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Proposition 41: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund. But really it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)
Proposition 42: No
Why we're endorsing
Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what the backers of this measure would have you believe. In reality, it’s just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax. You don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php)
Proposition 43: No endorsement
Why we're endorsing
Despite commanding far less attention than the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a question reverberating throughout the nation: Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work? We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements California’s broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)
Proposition 44: No
Why we're endorsing
On its surface, everything about Prop 44 on California’s November ballot looks appealing. But it creates a complex administrative and legal regime that will drain limited staff time and resources from nonprofit clinics while distracting from patient care.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php)
Proposition 45: No
Why we're endorsing
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, and some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45. But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22468905.php)
Advertisement
U.S. Congress
The editorial board recommends
U.S. House District 11: Scott Wiener Democrat State senator
Why we're endorsing
With Scott Wiener, San Franciscans would send the state’s most relentless and effective legislator to Washington to zero in on universal healthcare, humane immigration policies, protections for the LGBTQ community and preserving democracy from President Donald Trump. Connie Chan, meanwhile, has a policy agenda and legislative track record that’s as spotty as it is sparse.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
U.S. House District 14: Aisha Wahab Democrat Member of Congress ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
Congress in the age of Trump is no place to learn on the job. Wahab is the only candidate prepared for the gravity of the moment.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/aisha-wahab-district-14-california-22268931.php)

California has a thoughtful and thorough system in place for appointing judges. ## Summary
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals.

Whether it is better to vote "yes" or "no" on California Proposition 41 is a subjective policy choice with substantial arguments on both sides, and there is no factual consensus on how a voter should decide. As an AI, I remain neutral on electoral decisions and cannot take a side by answering with a simple "yes" or "no." 

Here is an overview of what Proposition 41 does and the key arguments supporting each position:

---

### What Proposition 41 Does

Proposition 41 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment on California's November 2026 ballot titled **"Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes."**

If passed, Proposition 41 would:
1. **Mandate Pre-Election and Recurring Audits:** Require the California State Auditor to audit programs proposed to receive funding from new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot (once 25% of required petition signatures are collected), with summaries published in the state Voter Information Guide. It also requires the State Auditor to conduct follow-up audits every four years for programs funded by newly approved special taxes.
2. **Enforce the State Spending Limit (Gann Limit):** Prohibit new state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, from exempting their revenues from the state's voter-approved spending limit.
3. **Interact with Proposition 40:** Under the California Constitution, if two conflicting measures pass on the same ballot, the one receiving more "yes" votes prevails on conflicting provisions. Because Proposition 40 (the proposed "Billionaire Tax Act") exempts its revenues from the Gann limit, Proposition 41 is structured to directly conflict with and potentially nullify Proposition 40 if Proposition 41 passes with a higher vote total.

---

### Arguments in Favor of Voting YES

* **Government Accountability and Transparency:** Supporters—including the California Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs), the California Taxpayers Association (CalTax), and various regional chambers of commerce—argue that Californians pay high taxes without sufficient oversight. They contend that requiring independent, public audits before and after special taxes are passed ensures government accountability, discourages wasteful spending, and gives voters clear data before voting on tax proposals.
* **Fiscal Discipline:** Proponents believe the state spending limit (the Gann limit) exists to keep state budget growth aligned with economic and population growth. They argue that ballot measures should not carve out exemptions to spending caps, as doing so leads to unsustainable government expansion.
* **Countering the Billionaire Wealth Tax:** Many business and taxpayer advocates argue that Proposition 40’s proposed wealth tax poses significant economic risks, including the potential flight of high earners, capital, and businesses from California. Voting "yes" on Proposition 41 serves as a safeguard to prevent Proposition 40 from taking effect.

---

### Arguments in Favor of Voting NO

* **Viewed as a "Poison Pill" Initiative:** Opponents—including SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), public healthcare advocates, and progressive leaders like Senator Bernie Sanders—argue that Proposition 41 was funded by wealthy opponents of Proposition 40 primarily as a maneuver to block a dedicated tax on billionaires intended to fund healthcare, Medicaid (Medi-Cal), and education.
* **Restricting State Funding Flexibility:** Opponents contend that applying rigid spending limits to new special taxes would prevent California from funding urgent needs or mitigating federal cuts to healthcare, nutrition, and social safety-net programs.
* **Administrative Burden on the State Auditor:** Critics argue that California already has established oversight and audit mechanisms. Requiring mandatory audits of proposed initiatives before they have even fully qualified for the ballot could overwhelm the State Auditor’s resources and create new bureaucratic obstacles for grassroots citizen initiatives.

---

### Summary

* A **YES** vote favors stricter auditing requirements for new special taxes, adherence to the state spending limit, and blocking or limiting measures like Proposition 40.
* A **NO** vote opposes placing these restrictions and spending caps on new special taxes, maintaining the current state spending limit rules and preserving the legal pathway for Proposition 40.

The decision comes down to each voter's personal priorities regarding state spending caps, tax policy, government oversight, and wealth taxation.

PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election
The San Francisco Chronicle Editorial Board’s endorsements for the California and S.F. Bay Area election on Nov. 3.
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) | Updated Nov. 2, 2026 4:37 p.m.
California’s November election is shaping up to be one of the most confusing in years for voters to navigate. There are 14 measures on the state ballot, many of them dense and extremely complicated tax policies. Unsurprisingly, polls show 80% of voters are frustrated and pessimistic about how this election will impact them. Voters in San Francisco and Oakland will also have to weigh in on hugely impactful charter reform ballot measures that could change the future of their cities.
In this kind of environment, details matter. And, yes, your vote matters.
The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board has spent months interviewing candidates, talking to experts, fact checking campaign promises and scrutinizing the issues in every statewide contest on the ballot, along with a group of consequential races in the Bay Area. These recommendations are made by Opinion writers and editors; newsroom reporters who cover the campaigns do not participate in endorsement decisions.
Below are the editorial board’s recommendations for the November 2026 election . We encourage readers to click through to the full endorsements to see the board’s reasoning and understand its decisions — so that you can be fully armed to make your own informed decisions.

California races
The editorial board recommends
Governor: Xavier Becerra Democrat Voting rights attorney
Why we're endorsing
The entire purpose of electing an experienced politician like Becerra is to feel confident that he will have the discernment to know which big ideas to go after and which to pass on, that he will arrive on the job with a meaningful, achievable agenda and actionable plans, and that he can communicate that agenda transparently and effectively to the public. We do not feel confident. All that said, Becerra’s Republican opponent, Steve Hilton — an ally of President Donald Trump — is no viable option.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-governor-race-22494871.php)
Lieutenant Governor: Fiona Ma Democrat State treasurer/CPA
Why we're endorsing
Fiona Ma comes with significant baggage — which is why she wasn’t our first choice for the role in the June primary. But she has the competence and experience to smoothly assume the duties of the state’s No. 2 office. Given the ramblings of her opponent, we cautiously recommend Ma for lieutenant governor.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/lieutenant-governor-california-state-election-22404751.php)
Secretary of State: Shirley Weber Democrat California secretary of state ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
California is no ocean of calm when it comes to elections. The need for steady and trustworthy leadership from our secretary of state cannot be understated. Shirley Weber’s breadth of experience, willingness to do the right thing and fierce advocacy for voting rights make her the strongest candidate.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/shirley-weber-secretary-state-california-22228493.php)
Controller: Malia Cohen Democrat State controller ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
The State Controller’s Office is California’s internal auditor — empowered to investigate how state agencies and local governments are spending state funds. Overall, we think Cohen has made enough progress to merit another term. But Californians should stay watchful to ensure she keeps the positive momentum going.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/malia-cohen-state-controller-california-22242981.php)
Treasurer: Eleni Kounalakis Democrat Lieutenant governor
Why we're endorsing
The California state treasurer is the main banker, financier and asset manager for the world’s fourth-largest economy. With her thorough grasp of the treasurer’s complex duties and the political gravitas to get things done, Eleni Kounalakis deserves your vote.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-eleni-kounalakis-california-treasurer-22154455.php)
Attorney General: Rob Bonta Democrat Attorney general ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
In our endorsement interview, incumbent Rob Bonta’s calm, clear and concise grasp of the complexities and nuances of California law — honed through more than eight years in the state Assembly — surpassed that of most of the current gubernatorial candidates.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/rob-bonta-attorney-general-california-22194540.php)
Insurance Commissioner: Ben Allen Democrat State senator
Why we're endorsing
The insurance market has began to show signs of recovery. Insurers are finally starting to write new policies in the state. Electing a rash insurance commissioner could reverse that progress and cause the market to implode. Ben Allen has what it takes to hold insurers accountable and regulate their market conduct while also fostering the conditions necessary to keep the market stable.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/insurance-commissioner-california-allen-kim-22321376.php)
Superintendent of Public Instruction: Richard Barrera School board member
Why we're endorsing
Richard Barrera is an increasingly rare California progressive who brings all parties to the table, a skill that the new state superintendent of public instruction will need as the role of the office changes.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/superintendent-richard-barrera-sonja-shaw-22376416.php)
State Board of Equalization District 1: It's complicated
Why we're endorsing
The Chronicle Editorial Board writes that the Board of Equalization shouldn’t exist.

California propositions
The editorial board recommends
Proposition 1: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Befitting the broad consensus on California’s affordability crisis, Prop 1 has no formal opposition. The measure is the product of years of legislative sausage-making and is unwieldy. But the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait — and Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop1-california-housing-vote-22442444.php)
Proposition 2: Yes
Why we're endorsing
If used to the fullest extent, Prop 2 could improve California’s budget stability, permitting the state to cover about 50% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years. Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-2-money-california-22468892.php)
Proposition 3: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but also keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php)
Proposition 4: No
Why we're endorsing
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends on how it’s designed. Prop 4 has a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)
Proposition 5: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials. The process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)
Proposition 37: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Prop 37 promises to make it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership. Its scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change the state’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php)
Proposition 38: No
Why we're endorsing
Wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world? Prop 38 positions itself as such a balm. In fact, it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years. It would give billions to an institute co-founded by billionaire Michael Milken, also known as the “junk bond king,” who was pardoned by Trump in 2020.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Proposition 39: No
Why we're endorsing
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. But even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California, Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-proposition-39-voter-fraud-california-22463918.php)
Proposition 40: No
Why we're endorsing
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be. Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” If it backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. No one is coming to save us, and it won’t be the wealthy who suffer. California isn’t a lab rat. Voters shouldn’t allow our state to be treated like one.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Proposition 41: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund. But really it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)
Proposition 42: No
Why we're endorsing
Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what the backers of this measure would have you believe. In reality, it’s just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax. You don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php)
Proposition 43: No endorsement
Why we're endorsing
Despite commanding far less attention than the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a question reverberating throughout the nation: Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work? We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements California’s broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)
Proposition 44: No
Why we're endorsing
On its surface, everything about Prop 44 on California’s November ballot looks appealing. But it creates a complex administrative and legal regime that will drain limited staff time and resources from nonprofit clinics while distracting from patient care.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php)
Proposition 45: No
Why we're endorsing
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, and some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45. But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22468905.php)

U.S. Congress
The editorial board recommends
U.S. House District 11: Scott Wiener Democrat State senator
Why we're endorsing
With Scott Wiener, San Franciscans would send the state’s most relentless and effective legislator to Washington to zero in on universal healthcare, humane immigration policies, protections for the LGBTQ community and preserving democracy from President Donald Trump. Connie Chan, meanwhile, has a policy agenda and legislative track record that’s as spotty as it is sparse.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
U.S. House District 14: Aisha Wahab Democrat Member of Congress ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
Congress in the age of Trump is no place to learn on the job. Wahab is the only candidate prepared for the gravity of the moment.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/aisha-wahab-district-14-california-22268931.php)

The editorial board recommends
Kelli M. Evans: Yes
Why we're endorsing
California has a thoughtful and thorough system in place for appointing judges. Every four years, voters are given the important yet perplexing job of deciding whether to retain a slate of judges who already serve. None of the justices up for retention in the November election have been cited for disciplinary matters on the Commission on Judicial Performance’s database, nor have our queries into their backgrounds turned up any red flags. We recommend a “yes” vote on all of them.

Billionaire tax proposed
On November 3, Californians will vote on Proposition 40.
The proposal, dubbed the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would put in place a one-time tax on high-wealth state residents as well as certain trusts.
Individuals and certain trusts worth $1 billion or more would be subject to an excise tax of up to 5%.
Importantly, the tax would apply to those who were California residents as of January 1, 2026.
Meanwhile, net worth would be determined as of a set asset 'valuation date' — December 31, 2026.
The ballot initiative would require California resident individuals to, when filing their 2026 tax return, declare that their net assets were worth 'less than or equal to' $1 billion as of the valuation date.
California residents subject to the tax also would need to submit a declaration of the amount of tax owed, along with supporting appraisals or evidence of fair market value used in their calculations.
The proposal would treat married couples as a single individual.

content.text:
Whether it is better to vote "yes" or "no" on California Proposition 41 is a subjective policy choice with substantial arguments on both sides, and there is no factual consensus on how a voter should decide. As an AI, I remain neutral on electoral decisions and cannot take a side by answering with a simple "yes" or "no." 

Here is an overview of what Proposition 41 does and the key arguments supporting each position:

---

### What Proposition 41 Does

Proposition 41 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment on California's November 2026 ballot titled **"Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes."**

If passed, Proposition 41 would:
1. **Mandate Pre-Election and Recurring Audits:** Require the California State Auditor to audit programs proposed to receive funding from new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot (once 25% of required petition signatures are collected), with summaries published in the state Voter Information Guide. It also requires the State Auditor to conduct follow-up audits every four years for programs funded by newly approved special taxes.
2. **Enforce the State Spending Limit (Gann Limit):** Prohibit new state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, from exempting their revenues from the state's voter-approved spending limit.
3. **Interact with Proposition 40:** Under the California Constitution, if two conflicting measures pass on the same ballot, the one receiving more "yes" votes prevails on conflicting provisions. Because Proposition 40 (the proposed "Billionaire Tax Act") exempts its revenues from the Gann limit, Proposition 41 is structured to directly conflict with and potentially nullify Proposition 40 if Proposition 41 passes with a higher vote total.

---

### Arguments in Favor of Voting YES

* **Government Accountability and Transparency:** Supporters—including the California Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs), the California Taxpayers Association (CalTax), and various regional chambers of commerce—argue that Californians pay high taxes without sufficient oversight. They contend that requiring independent, public audits before and after special taxes are passed ensures government accountability, discourages wasteful spending, and gives voters clear data before voting on tax proposals.
* **Fiscal Discipline:** Proponents believe the state spending limit (the Gann limit) exists to keep state budget growth aligned with economic and population growth. They argue that ballot measures should not carve out exemptions to spending caps, as doing so leads to unsustainable government expansion.
* **Countering the Billionaire Wealth Tax:** Many business and taxpayer advocates argue that Proposition 40’s proposed wealth tax poses significant economic risks, including the potential flight of high earners, capital, and businesses from California. Voting "yes" on Proposition 41 serves as a safeguard to prevent Proposition 40 from taking effect.

---

### Arguments in Favor of Voting NO

* **Viewed as a "Poison Pill" Initiative:** Opponents—including SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), public healthcare advocates, and progressive leaders like Senator Bernie Sanders—argue that Proposition 41 was funded by wealthy opponents of Proposition 40 primarily as a maneuver to block a dedicated tax on billionaires intended to fund healthcare, Medicaid (Medi-Cal), and education.
* **Restricting State Funding Flexibility:** Opponents contend that applying rigid spending limits to new special taxes would prevent California from funding urgent needs or mitigating federal cuts to healthcare, nutrition, and social safety-net programs.
* **Administrative Burden on the State Auditor:** Critics argue that California already has established oversight and audit mechanisms. Requiring mandatory audits of proposed initiatives before they have even fully qualified for the ballot could overwhelm the State Auditor’s resources and create new bureaucratic obstacles for grassroots citizen initiatives.

---

### Summary

* A **YES** vote favors stricter auditing requirements for new special taxes, adherence to the state spending limit, and blocking or limiting measures like Proposition 40.
* A **NO** vote opposes placing these restrictions and spending caps on new special taxes, maintaining the current state spending limit rules and preserving the legal pathway for Proposition 40.

The decision comes down to each voter's personal priorities regarding state spending caps, tax policy, government oversight, and wealth taxation.
